analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to sell individual health coverage to uninsured children regardless of health status.
analysis.headline: The bill won 39 cosponsors but never left a House subcommittee, and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required health insurers selling individual policies to accept any uninsured child under 16 who could not get coverage elsewhere, regardless of health or preexisting conditions, and to price children's premiums in line with their actuarial cost. It built directly on the 1996 HIPAA law, which gave similar guaranteed-access protections to certain adults who had lost group coverage. It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured children under 16 (born after September 30, 1983) who are U.S. citizens or lawfully residing, are not covered by a parent's employer plan, Medicare, Medicaid, or other insurance, and whose coverage was not previously cancelled for nonpayment or fraud. For these children, insurers could no longer turn them away or exclude their preexisting conditions, and premiums could not be set above a ratio tied to the coverage's actuarial value [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured children locked out of coverage

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees that every health insurance issuer in the individual market must offer coverage to an eligible uninsured child and may not deny enrollment, extending the HIPAA guaranteed-access framework to children [S3].

Bars the use of preexisting condition exclusions against eligible children, except to the limited extent HIPAA allows for non-late enrollees, so a child with asthma, diabetes, or another condition could not be shut out of coverage [S3].

Restricts premium setting: the ratio of an eligible child's premium to the premium for HIPAA-protected individuals could not exceed the ratio of the coverage's actuarial value for children versus those individuals, limiting insurer room to price sick children out [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance issuers in the individual market, which would have to accept children they would previously have declined or surcharged, spreading those costs across the individual-market risk pool. Families would still pay the premiums themselves; the bill provided no subsidies [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill guaranteed access to a policy but not the ability to afford one: it created no subsidies or cost assistance, so a low-income family could still be unable to pay the premium even though insurers had to offer coverage [S3].

By forcing insurers to cover children regardless of health status in the small individual market, the bill would likely raise premiums for other individual-market policyholders, since costs for higher-risk children would be spread across the pool [S3].
The requirement would not apply in states that implemented an 'acceptable alternative mechanism' under HIPAA section 2744, leaving children in those states without the federal guarantee [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit was real: children with preexisting conditions or no employer-sponsored option would gain a legal right to buy coverage rather than being turned away, closing a gap HIPAA left open for kids. But the bill addressed only half the problem — it forced insurers to offer policies without helping families pay for them — and its cost would land partly on other individual-market buyers through higher premiums. It also let states substitute weaker alternative mechanisms. A stronger design would have paired the access guarantee with affordability help, as the children's coverage efforts of that era eventually did.

outcome.mechanism: The House Commerce Committee never acted on it; after a routine referral to its Health and Environment Subcommittee, the bill sat there until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Elizabeth Furse introduced the bill on March 20, 1997, joined by seven original cosponsors including Reps. Stabenow, DeFazio, and Markey [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and on March 28, 1997 was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no subcommittee markup, no committee vote, no floor action, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Individual-market health insurers are better off because the bill died: they never had to accept uninsured children they could previously decline. Uninsured children with preexisting conditions gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Elizabeth Furse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend HIPAA-style guaranteed coverage access to uninsured children

for.name: 39 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a 40-member Democratic sponsor base

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley
against.what_they_did: Committee referred the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or committee vote; the bill received no action for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill was introduced by a Democrat; no Republican cosponsor is listed, and since the bill never reached a floor vote, no vote record exists — the partisan split shows up only in sponsorship.

industries.note: The bill would have forced issuers selling individual policies to accept any eligible uninsured child regardless of health status, restricted preexisting-condition exclusions, and capped how far children's premiums could exceed a standardized actuarial ratio — ending their ability to decline or price out high-risk children [S3]. Insurers avoided all of this when the bill died without action [S5].
